Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, meaning heat moves through it faster. That is why a thin aluminum pan heats up quickly and responds fast when you raise or lower the burner. But staying hot is not just about conductivity. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A cast-iron pan is usually much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. Because it has more mass, it can hold a larger amount of heat energy. Once it is hot, adding cold food does not cool it down as quickly. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat efficiently, but it has less stored heat to give.

For example, if you sear a cold steak, a hot cast-iron skillet often keeps sizzling after the steak hits the surface. A thin aluminum pan may lose temperature quickly, so the steak can steam or gray before browning well.

One limitation of the comparison is that pan design matters. A thick aluminum pan, especially one with a heavy base, can hold heat much better than a very thin one. So the difference is not only the metal, but also the pan’s thickness, weight, and construction.

Aluminum is great at moving heat, but that’s not the same as holding a lot of heat.

Think of heat like money. Aluminum is a fast spender: it takes heat from the burner and passes it along quickly to the food. Cast iron is more like a thick savings account. It takes longer to heat up because there’s so much heavy metal to warm, but once it’s hot, it has stored a lot of energy. So when you drop in a cold steak, a handful of mushrooms, or a wet batch of zucchini, the cast-iron pan’s temperature doesn’t crash as fast.

That’s why a cast-iron skillet can give you better browning on a steak. The meat pulls heat from the pan immediately, and the pan has enough thermal mass to keep searing instead of cooling down and steaming the surface. A thin aluminum pan may heat quickly, but it can lose temperature quickly too, especially if the food is cold or crowded.

One limitation: this comparison depends on thickness and construction. A thick aluminum pan, especially one with a heavy base, can hold plenty of heat, while a small, thin cast-iron pan won’t feel magically powerful. Conductivity matters; it’s just not the whole story.

The cast iron may conduct heat less efficiently, but because it is heavy, it can keep feeding heat into the steak and maintain a stronger sear.
